title: Place Value Builder
context: Grade 4, the opening topic of the large numbers chapter. An adult sees a place value chart being filled in. What the page is actually doing is growing the chart: a child who has only ever met four columns has to watch a fifth one open, and then a sixth and a seventh, before any of the reading and writing that follows will mean anything.

writeup.why: Build numbers bigger than any you have written before, and watch a new place open when there is nowhere left to put the extra one.
writeup.look: A chart of place value columns with a tray of numbered tokens below it, and the number you have built written out above.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Place Value Builder' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number as it stands, its digits in their period colours, redrawn every time a token lands or a bundle carries left, with the number of columns the chart now has written small beside it in ink. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The chart sits across the top of the working area, 1086 by 300 at 64,202: ruled columns 120 wide under headings 44 tall, the ones column pinned at the far right so that every new column opens to the left and no digit already written ever moves, four columns at the first sight of it and as many as seven by the end. Each column carries its place name in its heading, ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakhs and ten lakhs, and holds its tokens stacked from the floor of the column upwards, never more than nine of them standing. Under the chart a tray 1086 by 132 at 64,516 holds four stacks of token tiles: a one is a square 36 by 36, a ten a strip of ten of those squares standing on end at 36 by 72, a hundred a block ruled ten by ten at 72 by 72, and a thousand that same block drawn as a cube, each with its number printed on its face so a tile can be read as well as counted. A tenth token dropped into a column ties itself with a drawn band, turns into one tile of the next size and travels left along a carry lane 12 tall that runs under the column headings; at walking pace that takes one slow breath per column, so a cascade across four full columns is four of them in a row. The period bands lie behind the columns, ones deep blue over three places, thousands green over two and lakhs vermilion over two, each named above the headings, and a comma is written 40 tall in the gap between two columns, never inside one. A reading strip 1086 by 66 at the foot of the working area spells the number out in words one period at a time, each period in its own band colour. The number line, when it is opened, takes the tray's rectangle: a ruled strip with labelled ticks at the hundreds either side of the built number and the number itself dropped on it as an amber pin. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a number is asked for, and on the third and fourth phases a word pad of place and period names, ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakhs and ten lakhs, with thousands and lakhs doubling as the period names, so a new column can be named with one press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a digit takes the colour of its period, deep blue in the ones period, green in the thousands and vermilion in the lakhs, and rose in the millions where the international chart reaches; a digit under discussion, or the one that decides a comparison, is amber; a zero holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a place is told by its column heading and a period by its band before either is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the largest number the child built, its chart with the period bands, and that number written out in words.

phases.win: a new column opens on the left and catches the carry
phases.does: adds a single one token and watches every column turn over
phases.goal: the four nines roll over together and a fifth place opens
phases.says: Add one more. Watch every column, not just the last one.
phases.check: Away from the screen: what is one more than the greatest three digit number, and how many digits has your answer?
phases.feels: four columns all turn over together, and the chart itself has to get wider
phases.hands: Write the greatest four digit number on paper, add one to it by hand and let the answer be wrong before it is corrected. Then set out four saucers in a row with nine buttons in each, drop one more button into the saucer at the right, and trade ten for one of the next saucer along until the last saucer is full too.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the number. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many tokens are in the ones column now? Second rung, the phase's: what happens to a column the moment it reaches ten? Third rung: the chart is cut to two columns holding nine and nine and the child adds one to that. The pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: adding one has always touched the last digit and nothing else, which is true of every number the child has met so far.
wrong.move: turns over the ones column only and leaves the other three nines standing.
wrong.screen: the ten ones in the ones column bundle and the bundled token travels left, and the tens column is shown already holding nine; the running count holds still while that column is counted out to ten, one token at a time, and then bundles too. The child's number stays in the answer slot beside the chart.

wrong.why: the chart has four columns, and a chart with four columns has held every answer up to now.
wrong.move: says the answer must still be a four digit number.
wrong.screen: the last carry token is left sitting hard against the left edge of the chart with no column under it, and it stays there, not moving and not fading, while the four headings are read out from the right and run out. Nothing is cleared.

phases.screen: the chart holding the greatest four digit number in four full columns
phases.soWhat: When the last place is full, adding one more opens a new place.
phases.concept: One more than the biggest four digit number

phases.win: the counter reaches the target and the thousands column holds ten bundled tokens
phases.does: drags tokens until the counter reads the target number
phases.goal: a big number is still built from ones, tens, hundreds and thousands
phases.says: Build it with the tokens you have. How many thousand tokens did that take?
phases.check: How many thousand rupee notes would you need to make ten thousand?
phases.feels: ten tiles of the biggest kind you have, and they turn into one thing with a new name
phases.hands: Put out real money with nothing bigger than a hundred rupee note on the table and ask for ten thousand five hundred twelve to be counted out. Let the child find out for themselves how many notes ten thousand takes before anything is switched on.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the biggest tile in the tray? Second rung, the phase's: how many of those make one of the place to its left? Third rung: the target is cut back to a five digit number with zeros in its lower places, so only the thousands column has to be filled. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: every other place in the number has a tile of its own, so this place ought to have one too.
wrong.move: hunts the tray for a ten thousand tile.
wrong.screen: the four stacks lift in turn and name themselves, one, ten, one hundred, one thousand, and no fifth stack appears; then ten thousand tiles gather in the thousands column, bundle, and carry left into the ten thousands, where they land as one token. The child's answer stays in the answer slot.

wrong.why: the tiles go in fast and the number is written up at the top left, not under the hand that is dropping them.
wrong.move: drops thousand tiles past the target and keeps going.
wrong.screen: the chart counts its own thousands column out loud, one token lifting at a time, and the built number and the target number are laid one under the other in the same chart with their columns aligned, so the column holding too much shows itself. No token is taken out for the child.

phases.screen: an empty chart with the token tray full beneath it
phases.soWhat: A big number is still built out of ones, tens, hundreds and thousands.
phases.concept: Showing a big number with tokens

phases.win: the lakhs and then the ten lakhs columns appear and are named
phases.does: adds one more token at each ceiling and names the place that opens
phases.goal: every rollover opens exactly one more place to the left
phases.says: One more again. What is this new place called?
phases.check: One more than the greatest five digit number is one lakh. How many places has it, and what are they called?
phases.feels: the chart keeps opening one more room on the left, and the room always has a name
phases.hands: Write the greatest five digit number on paper, add one and say the answer out loud. Do the same with the greatest six digit number. Write both answers one under the other and count their places, not their zeros.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which column did the last token land in? Second rung, the phase's: what is written in that column's heading? Third rung: the headings are lit one at a time from the right and the child reads along until the lit one. The word pad of place names stays open.

wrong.why: five zeros in a row look like the number of thousands, and counting zeros has given the right answer often enough before.
wrong.move: calls one lakh ten thousand, counting the zeros instead of the places.
wrong.screen: the columns are read from the right, one heading lighting at a time, ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakhs, and the one token stops in the column whose heading is lit last. The child's name for it stays in the answer slot beside the chart's.

wrong.why: the new number looks far bigger than the one before it, so one extra column seems too small a change to explain it.
wrong.move: expects two new columns to open at once.
wrong.screen: the cascade runs again slowly and the single carry token coming out of the leftmost column is followed by a thin ink line to the one new column that opens to catch it; then the headings are counted along and come out one more than before.

phases.screen: the chart at the greatest five digit number, then the greatest six
phases.soWhat: Every rollover opens exactly one new place, and that place has its own name.
phases.concept: The chart grows a new place each time

phases.win: the number is spelled out in words and matches what the child said
phases.does: places the commas and then reads the number one period at a time
phases.goal: commas mark the periods, and the periods are how a number is read
phases.says: Read it in chunks, not digit by digit. Say the name of each chunk.
phases.check: Put the commas into a six digit number of your own and read it to me in chunks.
phases.feels: six digits that were a mouthful turn into three short chunks you can say
phases.hands: Find a large number on a bill or in a newspaper, copy its digits onto paper without the commas, and have the child put the commas in and read the number aloud in chunks.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: count three digits in from the right. Second rung, the phase's: how many digits go in the next group? Third rung: the period bands are switched on first and the child writes one comma at each band edge. The word pad of period names stays open.

wrong.why: the first comma went in after three digits, so every comma after it looks as though it should do the same.
wrong.move: groups the digits in threes all the way along.
wrong.screen: the comma the child wrote stays exactly where it was put, and the period bands slide in behind the columns, three places, then two, then two, so the bands and the commas sit on the stage disagreeing with each other; then the band edges are counted out from the right. Nothing is erased.

wrong.why: reading left to right one symbol at a time is how reading works everywhere else on a page.
wrong.move: reads the number digit by digit, naming each symbol in turn.
wrong.screen: the digits of one period lift together as a single piece and the reading strip writes that period and its name, then the next; each period stays lit until its name has been said, and the strip ends with three chunks where the child read six symbols.

phases.screen: a six digit number in the chart with the period bands behind it
phases.soWhat: Commas mark the periods, and the periods are how a number is read.
phases.concept: Commas split a number into periods

writeup.delight: The first phase, the moment the extra one token lands. All four nines turn over to zeros in turn, right to left, each one sending a bundled token left along the carry lane, and the last carry arrives at the edge of the chart with nowhere to go. It waits there a beat. Then the chart draws itself one column wider, the heading writes itself as ten thousands, and the token settles into the new column. Nothing else moves and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the chart stands four columns wide with nine tokens in every one of them, the greatest four digit number already built, and a single loose one token waits on the tray below. On the second the chart is ruled and empty and the tray is full, four stacks of tiles marked one, ten, one hundred and one thousand. On the third the chart stands five columns wide and full of nines. On the fourth a six digit number is already in the chart with the three period bands lying behind it and not one comma written yet. The running count at the top left holds the number as it stands, and the answer slot and the pad wait empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the loose one token on the tray, or the first empty column, or the gap where the first comma will go, gives one slow pulse while the voice says there is one more to drop in. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any tokens, any number as far as ten lakh, with the periods, the commas and the number line switched on or off. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on building numbers past four digits, naming the places and marking the periods.
voiceLines: A chart, a tray of tokens, and one more to drop in.
Add one more. Watch every column, not just the last one.
Build it with the tokens you have. How many thousand tokens did that take?
One more again. What is this new place called?
Read it in chunks, not digit by digit. Say the name of each chunk.
Same chart. It may not be the same width any more.
Free play. Any tokens, any number, commas on or off.
Lay them in again, slowly. Watch what leaves the column.
You grew the chart three times, and named every place that opened.

observations.why: Ten of anything in one column is exactly one of the column to its left.
observations.soWhat: A column never holds ten, so it hands the ten on and empties.
observations.observe: Nine ones and one more left the ones column with nothing standing in it.

observations.why: The last carry had no column to land in, so a place opened to catch it.
observations.soWhat: A number grows a new place when the places it has have run out of room.
observations.observe: Every column turned over at once and the chart came out one column wider.

observations.why: There is no ten thousand tile in the tray, only a thousand.
observations.soWhat: Ten thousand is ten thousands, which is what the new place is named after.
observations.observe: The thousands column took ten tokens before anything was worth ten thousand.

observations.why: A comma marks where one period ends and the next begins.
observations.soWhat: A number is read one period at a time, each with its own name.
observations.observe: The commas turned six digits into three short chunks to say.

source_tool.description: A mat of place value columns fills the stage and a tray of token tiles sits beneath it, marked one, ten, one hundred and one thousand. Dropping tokens into a column builds a number, and as soon as ten gather in one column they tie themselves into a single token of the next size and move left. A counter above the mat reads the number as it stands. Held at the greatest four digit number and given one more token, the counter rolls every nine over at once and the chart grows a ten thousands column to catch the carry, and the same thing happens again at the greatest five and six digit numbers. Once a number is built, period bands slide in behind the columns and commas appear at their boundaries, and the number is spelled out in words along the bottom. A number line strip can be opened to locate the built number between its neighbours.
source_tool.art_direction: A token tray under a growing chart / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.
Drawn things, not abstract boxes: token tiles, place value charts with ruled columns, a number line with labelled ticks, digit cards that can be picked up, and lettered tiles for the Roman numerals.

A large number is always shown with its digits sitting in named places, with the period bands behind them and the commas drawn where the Indian system puts them. A bare numeral with no chart behind it is never used to teach place value.
Where tokens or blocks stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A place is told apart by its column label first and by its band colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a token or a place the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The ones period is deep blue, the thousands period is green and the lakhs period is vermilion, and those three bands are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The millions period is rose and appears only where the international chart does. A digit under discussion, or the digit that decides a comparison, is amber. A zero holding an empty place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a period is told apart by its band and its label before its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Lay them in again, slowly. Watch what leaves the column.
voice.onNext: Same chart. It may not be the same width any more.
voice.opening: A chart, a tray of tokens, and one more to drop in.
voice.onFinish: You grew the chart three times, and named every place that opened.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any tokens, any number, commas on or off.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

Showing a big number with tokens
The chart grows a new place each time

placement.where: After the greatest four digit number has been written on paper and one more has been added by hand. The tool is what lets the rollover be watched rather than worked out.

answer_key.rule: Ten in any column bundle into one of the next column to the left. When the leftmost column is full, a new place opens for the carry, which is how 9999 becomes 10,000 and 99,999 becomes 1,00,000. The places are grouped into periods of three, then two, then two, and a comma is written at each boundary. A number is read one period at a time, each followed by its name except the ones.
answer_key.wrong: The tokens are laid out again one at a time, slowly, so the bundling can be watched as it happens. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Nine ones and one more make ten, so the ones column empties and one goes to the tens.
The same thing happens at the tens, the hundreds and then the thousands.
The last carry has no column to go to, so a ten thousands place opens.
items.answer: 10,000, and a fifth place has opened to hold it
items.question: The chart holds 9999 and one more token is dropped in. What does the counter read now?
items.checkpoint: Four nines roll over at once and a fifth place has to open.
items.misconception: Turning over only the ones column and writing 99,910.

steps: Ten thousand is ten of the thousand tokens, bundled.
Five hundred tokens fill the hundreds column.
One ten token and two one tokens finish the number.
items.answer: Ten, because there is no single token worth ten thousand
items.question: How many thousand tokens does it take to build 10,512?
items.checkpoint: Ten of the thousand tokens is exactly what a ten thousands place means.
items.misconception: Looking for a ten thousand token, when the tray holds no such tile.

steps: All five nines turn over to zero, one column at a time.
The carry coming out of the ten thousands needs a sixth column.
That column is the lakhs, so the number is 1,00,000, read as one lakh.
items.answer: The lakhs place opens, and the number is one lakh
items.question: The chart holds 99,999 and one more token is added. Which place opens, and what is the number called?
items.checkpoint: Every rollover opens exactly one more place on the left.
items.misconception: Calling 1,00,000 ten thousand, by counting its zeros instead of its places.

steps: Count three digits from the right and write the first comma there.
Count two more digits and write the second comma.
Read each period with its name, starting from the left.
items.answer: 7,38,000, read as seven lakh thirty-eight thousand
items.question: Put the commas into 738000 and then read the number aloud.
items.checkpoint: Commas mark where one period ends and the next begins.
items.misconception: Grouping in threes all the way along and writing 738,000.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: The greatest four digit number is 9999. What is its successor?
items.final_answer: 10,000, which is the smallest five digit number

items.question: How many digits has the smallest five digit number, and what is it?
Which tokens would you use to build 10,204?

items.question: A number line runs from 10000 to 11000 in steps of one hundred. Where does 10,512 sit?

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: drops a one, ten, hundred or thousand token into the chart
adds a single one token, which is what forces a rollover
ties ten tokens into one of the next size at walking pace
slides the ones, thousands and lakhs bands in behind the columns
writes a comma at each period boundary and takes them away again
spells the built number in words along the bottom of the stage
opens a strip and marks where the built number sits between its neighbours

teaching_notes: Write the greatest four digit number on paper first and add one to it by hand, and let them get it wrong. The tool is what lets the rollover be watched rather than reasoned about, and it is the whole of this topic. Use the bundle slowly control every time for the first few numbers; at full speed the carry is invisible and the child learns a rule instead of a reason. When the commas go in, insist on reading the number out loud in chunks. A number read digit by digit has not been read at all.
generation_prompt: Build a place value tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A chart of ruled place value columns that can grow from four columns to seven, with a tray of draggable token tiles marked one, ten, one hundred and one thousand beneath it. Dropping ten tokens into any column bundles them into a single token of the next size and moves it left, with a slow mode that animates the bundle at walking pace. A counter above the chart reads the current value. An add one more control drops a single one token, which at 9999, 99,999 and 9,99,999 cascades the carry across every column and grows a new column to catch it. Period bands for ones, thousands and lakhs slide in behind the columns and a comma control writes commas at the Indian boundaries of three, two and two. A read it out control spells the built number in words along the footer. A number line strip opens to mark the built number between its neighbouring hundreds. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Drag tokens onto the chart to build a number. When ten gather in one column they bundle and move left. Add one more token to a full chart and watch a new place open. Then switch the commas on and read your number aloud.
